sections.skill: Compare arguments by their evidence and values without treating disputed views as fact

questions.prompt: What two things do AI debates often mix?
questions.intro: Debates about AI's role, for example in schools, art, medicine or work, often mix two things: EVIDENCE (what is true or likely) and VALUES (what matters most). Someone may favor AI tutors because studies show gains (evidence) and because they value access for all (value). Someone else may worry about lost skills (evidence question) and value human connection (value). To weigh arguments fairly, separate the two: check the evidence, name the values, and notice when a disputed view is presented as settled fact.

sections.skill: Sort claims into evidence and values

questions.prompt: "AI reads scans faster" is which kind?
questions.intro: For each claim, ask: Could it be checked with data or observation? If yes, it is an EVIDENCE claim (true or false, strong or weak). If it is about what matters, what is good or what should be prioritized, it is a VALUE claim. Example debate about AI in hospitals: "AI reads scans faster" (evidence). "Speed matters more than cost" (value). "Patients deserve to know when AI is used" (value). "Most patients want to know" (evidence, checkable by surveys).

sections.skill: Handle limited evidence and good-faith disagreement

questions.prompt: Evidence about a new AI use is early and mixed. What kind of conclusion is honest?

choices.text: A final and certain conclusion, which should never be revisited even when new evidence appears

questions.intro: Good-faith disagreement is normal when people share facts but weigh values differently. Evidence can be limited, early or mixed, so honest conclusions are often provisional. Watch for cherry-picking (only citing supportive studies), treating predictions as facts, and dismissing people instead of arguments. A fair summary states the strongest version of each side. This course does not tell you which side to take.

questions.prompt: Is good-faith disagreement possible when people share the facts?

choices.text: Yes, if they weigh values differently
